subject: Biology
title: Why the Ocean Matters
description: A short lesson to help you apply Why the Ocean Matters.

hook.text: The ocean covers 71% of Earth's surface, yet we've explored less of it than the surface of Mars.

buildup.text: Oceans regulate climate, produce over half the world's oxygen, and absorb a quarter of human CO₂ emissions.

discovery.text: Phytoplankton—microscopic ocean plants—generate more oxygen than all terrestrial forests combined.

twist.text: We have better maps of the Moon than of the ocean floor. Over 80% remains unmapped.

climax.text: The ocean is Earth's life-support system—and we're only beginning to understand it.

punchline.text: Planet Earth should really be called Planet Ocean.

quiz.question: What produces more oxygen than all forests combined?

details.summary: The ocean covers 71 percent of Earth's surface, produces over half the world's oxygen, absorbs 30 percent of human CO2 emissions, and regulates global climate through heat distribution. It provides food for over 3 billion people and supports economies worth trillions of dollars.
details.whyItMatters: Despite its critical importance, the ocean is threatened by warming, acidification, overfishing, and pollution simultaneously. Understanding the ocean's vital role is essential for motivating the protection it urgently needs.
takeaways: Oceans produce over 50 percent of Earth's oxygen via phytoplankton photosynthesis
Over 3 billion people depend on the ocean as their primary protein source
The ocean has absorbed over 90 percent of excess heat from climate change

faq.question: How does the ocean regulate Earth's climate?
faq.answer: The ocean absorbs over 90 percent of excess heat from greenhouse gases and about 30 percent of CO2 emissions. Currents redistribute tropical heat toward the poles. Evaporation from the ocean drives weather systems. Without the ocean, Earth's climate would be far more extreme.

faq.question: How much of the ocean has been explored?
faq.answer: Only about 5 percent of the ocean has been explored in detail. More of the Moon's surface has been mapped at high resolution than the ocean floor. New species, ecosystems, and geological features are discovered on virtually every deep-sea expedition.
